lesson.title: Running Subnetting in Reverse: Supernetting and Route Aggregation
lesson.summary: Supernetting combines multiple smaller, contiguous network blocks into one larger block advertised with a shorter prefix, doing the opposite of subnetting to shrink routing tables and simplify address announcements.
lesson.body:
If subnetting borrows host bits to make a network smaller by lengthening its prefix, supernetting does the reverse: it lends bits back to the host portion by shortening the prefix, merging several smaller, contiguous, same-sized blocks into one larger block described by a single CIDR prefix. The technique depends entirely on CIDR notation, because classful addressing had no concept of a prefix shorter than the fixed class boundary. Supernetting is also called route aggregation or route summarization, and it exists mainly to solve a scaling problem: without it, every small block an ISP hands out to a customer would need its own separate entry in every backbone router's routing table, and by the early 1990s that table was growing fast enough to threaten router memory and processing limits.

The core requirement for supernetting is that the blocks being merged must be contiguous in address space and properly aligned on a power-of-two boundary. Consider four /24 blocks: 208.130.28.0/24, 208.130.29.0/24, 208.130.30.0/24, and 208.130.31.0/24. Written in binary, the third octet values are 00011100, 00011101, 00011110, and 00011111; the first 6 bits, 000111, are identical across all four, and only the last 2 bits vary, covering all four combinations 00, 01, 10, and 11. That means these four /24 blocks can be summarized as a single 208.130.28.0/22, a supernet with 22 network bits and 10 host bits, holding 1024 addresses total, exactly the four /24 blocks combined, since 4 times 256 equals 1024. A router that would otherwise need four routing table entries can instead advertise just one.

This only works cleanly because the blocks align on the boundary implied by the shorter prefix; four arbitrary /24 blocks scattered across unrelated address ranges cannot be supernetted into one prefix, because a single CIDR block always represents a mathematically contiguous, power-of-two-aligned range, never an arbitrary collection. Internet service providers rely on supernetting constantly: a provider that owns a /16 block can subnet pieces of it out to individual customers as /24s or smaller, yet still advertise the entire /16 as one route to the rest of the internet, hiding all of that internal structure from external routers. This is the same logic, run at a larger scale, that a CIDR summary like a /23 achieves by combining two /24s.

Supernetting is a core reason the modern internet's routing tables remain manageable despite the huge number of individually allocated address blocks in existence. Where subnetting is a tool an organization uses internally to organize and isolate its own hosts, supernetting is largely a tool used at the boundaries between networks and by internet service providers, letting the messy internal detail of thousands of subnets collapse into a small number of externally visible routes.

Both techniques are really the same underlying operation, moving the prefix boundary left or right along the 32 bits of an address, applied in opposite directions for opposite purposes: subnetting lengthens a prefix to create smaller, isolated pieces, and supernetting shortens a prefix to collapse pieces back into one larger, more efficiently advertised whole.
